deep_html:
TL;DR

  • Computers talk using IP addresses (142.250.183.14), humans type names (google.com). DNS turns one into the other.
  • Your browser asks a resolver, which walks a chain of servers: root → TLD (.com) → the domain's own name server.
  • Every answer comes with a TTL (time to live). Everyone along the way caches it until it expires. That is why DNS is fast most of the time, and why changes take time to reach everyone.

The analogy

Think of your phone's contacts app. You tap "Mom", the phone dials +91 98xxx xxxxx. You never remember the number; the app does.

DNS is the contacts app of the internet, except nobody has the full list. So when your browser meets a name it hasn't seen, it has to ask around: first a general directory that knows who handles .com names, then the .com office that knows who handles google.com, then Google's own server that finally says the number.

How it actually works

When you type www.example.com and press Enter, your browser does not go to the internet straight away. It checks the cheapest places first:

  1. Browser cache. Chrome remembers recent answers for a short while.
  2. Operating system cache (and the hosts file on your laptop).
  3. The recursive resolver. Usually run by your ISP (Jio, Airtel) or a public one like 8.8.8.8 (Google) or 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare). This server does the legwork for you.

If the resolver doesn't have the answer cached, it walks the tree:

  • Root servers know who runs every top-level domain (.com, .in, .org). There are 13 named root server identities, each copied to hundreds of locations worldwide.
  • TLD servers know which name servers are in charge of each domain under them.
  • The authoritative name server is the one the domain owner controls (Cloudflare, Route 53, GoDaddy…). It holds the real records.

The resolver remembers every step. The next person asking for any .com name skips the root, and anyone asking for example.com within the TTL gets an instant answer.

The records you'll actually meet

Record Maps Example
A name → IPv4 address example.com → 93.184.215.14
AAAA name → IPv6 address example.com → 2606:2800:…
CNAME name → another name (alias) www.shop.com → shop.netlify.app
MX where email for the domain goes → mail.google.com
TXT free text, used for verification Google / SPF verification strings
NS which servers are authoritative → ns1.cloudflare.com

TTL: the reason "DNS propagation" exists

Each answer says how long it may be cached, for example TTL 3600 = one hour. If you move your site to a new server and update the A record, people whose resolver cached the old answer keep going to the old server until their copy expires. Nothing is "propagating"; old caches are simply timing out.

Why frontend engineers should care

A DNS lookup on a cold cache costs anything from ~20 ms to a few hundred ms, and it happens before a single byte of your page can download. Every new domain your page uses (fonts, analytics, ad scripts, an image CDN) can cost another lookup.

You can tell the browser to start early:

<!-- Look up the name early (cheap) -->
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com">
<!-- Look up + connect (TCP + TLS) early: use for the 1–3 domains you will definitely hit -->
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>

See it yourself

  • Terminal: nslookup google.com or dig google.com (shows the TTL counting down if you run it twice).
  • Trace the full walk: dig +trace google.com.
  • Chrome DevTools → Network → click the first request → Timing tab → the DNS Lookup bar. Reload with cache disabled to see it grow.

Real-world story

On 4 October 2021, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp disappeared for about six hours. A maintenance command cut Facebook's data centers off, and its DNS servers, built to step back when they couldn't reach the data centers, withdrew themselves from the internet. With nobody able to answer "where is facebook.com?", the apps simply couldn't be found. (We made a reel about it: The day Facebook vanished.)

Common mistakes

  • Changing DNS with a long TTL. Lower the TTL (say to 300 s) a day before a migration, switch, then raise it again.
  • Putting a CNAME on the root domain (example.com itself). The standard doesn't allow it next to other records; use your provider's ALIAS/"CNAME flattening" instead.
  • Assuming DNS is free. Third-party scripts on five different domains = five lookups on a slow phone network.

Interview questions

Walk me through what DNS does when I type a URL.

Browser cache → OS cache/hosts file → recursive resolver. On a miss, the resolver asks a root server (which points to the TLD servers), then the TLD server (which points to the domain's authoritative servers), then the authoritative server, which returns the record with a TTL. Every layer caches the answer.

Recursive vs iterative queries?

Your device sends a recursive query: "give me the final answer". The resolver then makes iterative queries to root, TLD and authoritative servers, each of which only points to the next server.

Does DNS use UDP or TCP?

Mostly UDP on port 53, because it's one small question and one small answer. It falls back to TCP for large responses and zone transfers. Newer setups use DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or over TLS (DoT) to encrypt lookups.

A vs CNAME?

A points a name straight at an IP address. CNAME points a name at another name, which then has to be resolved too (an extra step, but you only update one place when the target's IP changes).

How can a frontend reduce DNS cost?

Use fewer third-party domains, self-host fonts and critical scripts, and add dns-prefetch/preconnect for the few domains you can't avoid.

title: TCP handshake
text: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK = 1 round trip before any data (e.g. ~200 ms India ↔ US). Keep-alive reuses connections; later requests show 0 ms "Initial connection". Trap: TCP guarantees order, so one lost packet blocks everything behind it (head-of-line blocking) → why HTTP/3 exists.
html:
• SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK = 1 round trip before any data (e.g. ~200 ms India ↔ US).
  • Keep-alive reuses connections; later requests show 0 ms "Initial connection".
  • Trap: TCP guarantees order, so one lost packet blocks everything behind it (head-of-line blocking) → why HTTP/3 exists.

title: HTTPS & the padlock
text: HTTPS = HTTP over TLS. 3 promises: encryption, integrity, authentication . Certificate chain: root CA (trusted by browser) → intermediate → site. TLS 1.3 handshake = 1 round trip (TLS 1.2 = 2). Trap: padlock = private connection, not a safe site. Phishing sites have valid certs.
html:
• HTTPS = HTTP over TLS. 3 promises: encryption, integrity, authentication.
  • Certificate chain: root CA (trusted by browser) → intermediate → site. TLS 1.3 handshake = 1 round trip (TLS 1.2 = 2).
  • Trap: padlock = private connection, not a safe site. Phishing sites have valid certs.

title: HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3
text: 1.1: one request per connection at a time → ~6 connections per site. 2: multiplexing + header compression on ONE TCP connection — but a lost packet stalls all streams. 3: QUIC over UDP, independent streams, survives Wi-Fi → mobile switches. Trap: HTTP/2 isn't always faster on lossy networks.
html:
• 1.1: one request per connection at a time → ~6 connections per site.
  • 2: multiplexing + header compression on ONE TCP connection — but a lost packet stalls all streams.
  • 3: QUIC over UDP, independent streams, survives Wi-Fi → mobile switches. Trap: HTTP/2 isn't always faster on lossy networks.

title: Reflow vs repaint
text: Geometry (width/height/top) → layout + paint + composite. Color → paint + composite. transform/opacity → composite only. Reflow spreads to siblings/parents. DevTools → Rendering → Paint flashing. Trap: reading offsetHeight right after a style write forces synchronous layout.

title: Layout thrashing
text: Read/write/read/write in a loop → a layout per read. Fix: batch all reads, then all writes; schedule writes in requestAnimationFrame . Shows as "Forced reflow is a likely performance bottleneck" in Performance. Q: layout-forcing reads: offsetHeight/Top, clientWidth, scrollTop, getBoundingClientRect().

title: One-chef kitchen
text: JS runs on one main thread that also does style, layout, paint. A 3 s loop freezes everything. Waiting (timers, fetch, events) happens in browser Web APIs; results come back through queues. Trap: setTimeout(fn, 0) = "as soon as possible", not "now".
html:
• JS runs on one main thread that also does style, layout, paint. A 3 s loop freezes everything.
  • Waiting (timers, fetch, events) happens in browser Web APIs; results come back through queues.
  • Trap: setTimeout(fn, 0) = "as soon as possible", not "now".
deep_html:
TL;DR

  • JavaScript in the browser runs on one main thread: one "chef" who also handles clicks, scrolling, style, layout and paint.
  • Waiting (timers, network, events) happens outside the chef, in the browser's Web APIs. Computing happens on the chef.
  • So a fetch() never freezes the page, but a long loop does. Anything over ~50 ms on the main thread is a long task, and users feel it.

The analogy

A restaurant with exactly one cook. The cook makes your food, but also takes orders, plates dishes and wipes the counter. If one order takes the cook 3 minutes of chopping, every other table waits, even the person who just wants water.

The cook does have helpers: a timer on the oven, a delivery boy who fetches ingredients. They work on their own and leave a note on the counter when done. The cook reads the notes only when the hands are free.

How it actually works

The main thread runs one piece of work at a time. Here's the loop it repeats forever:

Meanwhile the Web APIs (timers, network, input) work on their own and drop finished jobs into the task queue.

  • Call stack: the function the chef is running right now, and the functions that called it.
  • Web APIs: the helpers. setTimeout, fetch, DOM events and so on are handled by the browser, not by your JavaScript.
  • Task queue: finished helper jobs waiting for the chef (a timer fired, a click happened, a response arrived).
  • Rendering: the browser tries to draw ~60 times a second (every ~16.7 ms), but only between tasks. If your task runs 3 seconds, no frames are drawn for 3 seconds. That's the "frozen" page.

Blocking vs not blocking

// Freezes the page for 3 seconds: the chef never gets a break.
const end = Date.now() + 3000;
while (Date.now() < end) {}

// Doesn't freeze anything: the waiting happens in the browser, not on the chef.
fetch('/api/orders').then(r => r.json()).then(render);
setTimeout(() => console.log('3 seconds later'), 3000);

How to do heavy work without freezing

1. Break it into chunks and give the chef a break between them:

async function processAll(items) {
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    heavyWork(items[i]);
    if (i % 200 === 0) {
      // Let clicks, scroll and paint happen, then continue.
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));
    }
  }
}

2. Hire a second chef with a Web Worker, which runs on a separate thread (it can't touch the DOM, but it can crunch numbers):

// main.js
const worker = new Worker('worker.js');
worker.postMessage(bigArray);
worker.onmessage = e => showResult(e.data);

// worker.js
onmessage = e => postMessage(expensiveCalculation(e.data));

See it yourself

  • Open any site, paste the 3-second while loop in the Console, then try to scroll or click. Nothing responds until it ends.
  • DevTools → Performance → record while it runs. You'll see one long grey/yellow block with a red triangle: a long task.

Real-world connection

Google's INP (Interaction to Next Paint) metric, one of the Core Web Vitals, measures exactly this: how long after a tap the page actually paints a response. Busy main threads are the #1 cause of bad INP.

Common mistakes

  • "async makes it run in the background." It doesn't. An async function still runs on the main thread; only the waiting (await fetch) is offloaded.
  • Thinking setTimeout(fn, 0) runs now. It means "add a task as soon as possible". It still waits for the current task (and all microtasks) to finish.
  • Parsing a huge JSON or sorting 1 lakh rows in a click handler. Chunk it, move it to a worker, or do it on the server.

Interview questions

Is JavaScript single-threaded? Then how does fetch not block?

Your JavaScript runs on one thread, but the browser is multi-threaded. fetch hands the request to the browser's network layer; when the response arrives, a callback is queued and runs when the main thread is free.

What's the output order? 
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
console.log('D');

A, D, C, B. Synchronous code first (A, D). Then all microtasks (the promise: C). Then the next task (the timer: B).

What is a long task and why does it matter?

Any task that keeps the main thread busy for more than 50 ms. During it the page can't respond to input or paint, so clicks feel laggy. It directly hurts INP.

How would you keep the UI responsive while processing a large dataset?

Split the work into chunks and yield between them (setTimeout, or scheduler.yield() where supported), move pure computation to a Web Worker, or paginate/virtualise so you don't process everything at once.

title: Call stack & task queue
text: log A; setTimeout(log B, 0); log C → A, C, B. Stack runs sync code; Web APIs hold timers; callbacks wait in the task queue; event loop moves a task when the stack is empty. Q: no true 0 ms — deeply nested timers clamp to ≥ 4 ms.

• log A; setTimeout(log B, 0); log C → A, C, B.
  • Stack runs sync code; Web APIs hold timers; callbacks wait in the task queue; event loop moves a task when the stack is empty.
  • Q: no true 0 ms — deeply nested timers clamp to ≥ 4 ms.

title: Microtasks vs tasks
text: Tasks: timers, events. Microtasks: promise callbacks, queueMicrotask . After each task the loop drains ALL microtasks (incl. new ones), then may render, then next task. 1,timeout 2,promise 3,4 → 1 4 3 2. Trap: microtask starvation freezes the page.

  • Trap: microtask starvation freezes the page.

title: 16 ms frame budget
text: 60 Hz ≈ 16.7 ms per frame (120 Hz ≈ 8.3 ms). Keep your JS ≲ 10 ms. requestAnimationFrame runs right before paint, once per frame, pauses in background tabs. Use its timestamp (time-based motion). setInterval drifts against frames.

title: Long tasks
text: 50 ms = long task; blocks input. 100 ms feels instant (50 task + 50 input/paint). Fix: chunk work and yield ( await scheduler.yield() or setTimeout ). Metric: INP (Interaction to Next Paint), Core Web Vital since 2024 (replaced FID).

title: Bubbling & capturing
text: Phases: capture ↓ → target → bubble ↑. Listeners default to bubble; { capture: true } for capture. stopPropagation (stop the journey) ≠ preventDefault (stop default action). target = clicked element, currentTarget = element whose listener runs. focus/blur/mouseenter/mouseleave don't bubble.

title: Event delegation
text: One listener on the parent + e.target.closest('.row') . Fewer listeners, works for rows added later, no listener leaks. DevTools → Event Listeners → Ancestors. Trap: needs bubbling events; a child's stopPropagation hides it.

title: Memory leaks
text: GC frees what's unreachable from roots; a leak is unneeded but still reachable memory. Suspects: listeners not removed, intervals after unmount, ever-growing caches, detached DOM nodes. Use useEffect cleanup, WeakMap. Memory panel: compare heap snapshots, filter "Detached". Closures keep captured variables alive.

title: Observers
text: IntersectionObserver (lazy load, infinite scroll, autoplay, impressions), ResizeObserver, MutationObserver, PerformanceObserver. Better than scroll listeners: browser computes intersections, no forced layout in your code, fires only on threshold crossings.

title: White screen first
text: Every strategy answers one question: who builds the HTML, and when? Server (before sending) or browser (after arriving). Server-rendered: HTML has content → paint now, JS later. Big bundles take seconds to parse/run on cheap CPUs → throttle CPU (4x) too.

Trap: SSR isn't always faster — slow DB or far server = huge TTFB, and still not interactive until JS. SSR moves work, doesn't delete it.

title: Hydration mismatch
text:
Rule: server HTML must equal the browser's first render. Causes: Date , Math.random() , window / localStorage in render, timezone/locale, invalid nesting (
in

), extensions. Fix: same placeholder on both sides → fill browser-only values in useEffect . Tiny diffs: suppressHydrationWarning . Trap: typeof window checks in render CAUSE mismatches.

title: Visible but not clickable

title: Selective hydration
text: Classic hydration is all-or-nothing. React 18 hydrates each <Suspense> boundary independently, yielding between chunks. Clicking an un-hydrated part → React hydrates it first, then replays the click. Trap: it doesn't make JS smaller — same code downloads and runs; only order + chunking change.

title: Streaming SSR
text: Send the shell + fallbacks first; stream the slow parts later with a tiny script that swaps them in. React: renderToPipeableStream(<App />, { onShellReady() { stream.pipe(res) } }) . Works because HTTP bodies arrive in pieces (chunked in 1.1, DATA frames in 2/3). See it: Timing → long "Content Download"; View Source → <div hidden id="S:0"> + $RC(...) scripts. Trap: once the first chunk is out, status/headers are sent → no 404/redirect later. Decide before the shell.

title: React Server Components (RSC)
text: Run only on the server; can be async and read the DB; their code never ships. Only output (RSC payload) does. Interactive parts = 'use client' components; only those ship JS. See it: nextjs.org → Network → ?_rsc= requests on navigation. RSC ≠ SSR: SSR = HTML for first load, then everything hydrates. RSC never hydrates, refetchable on navigation. Frameworks use both. Trap: no useState / onClick in server components → pass data as props to a client component.

title: Resumability

Trap: first interaction must fetch code → slow on bad networks; mitigate by prefetching likely handlers.

Trap: edge render + single-region DB = every query crosses the planet. Only helps when data is close or cached.

title: 100 ms = money

Trap: averages hide slow users → report p75 .

title: LCP

Candidates: , video poster, CSS background image, text blocks. 4 parts: TTFB → resource load delay → load duration → render delay. Usually the delay (image found late) is the problem. See it: Performance panel → LCP marker + LCP breakdown insight. Trap: loading="lazy" on the hero makes LCP worse.

title: CLS
text: Sum of unexpected shifts; each = impact × distance; grouped into bursts (session windows); your worst burst = CLS. Culprits: images without width/height, ads/embeds without reserved space, injected banners, font swaps. Fix: reserve space ( width/height , aspect-ratio , min-height ). See it: Rendering → Layout Shift Regions. Trap: shifts within 500 ms of a tap/keypress are excluded; transform animations never shift layout.

deep_html:
TL;DR

  • CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures how much visible content moves unexpectedly while someone uses the page.
  • Good ≤ 0.1, poor > 0.25. It's one of Google's three Core Web Vitals, with LCP (loading) and INP (responsiveness).
  • Almost every shift has the same fix: reserve the space before the content arrives.

The analogy

Someone pulls your chair away just as you sit down. The chair was fine; it just moved at the worst moment. That's a layout shift: you aim for "Cancel", an ad loads above it, everything slides down, and your thumb lands on "Buy".

How it actually works

Each time a visible element moves without the user causing it, the browser records a layout shift and gives it a score:

shift score = impact fraction × distance fraction

  • Impact fraction: how much of the viewport the moving elements touched (before + after positions combined).
  • Distance fraction: how far they moved, as a fraction of the viewport's height (or width).

Example: an article covers 50% of the screen. A banner loads above it and pushes it down by 25% of the screen height. The article now touches 75% of the viewport (old + new area), so impact = 0.75, distance = 0.25 → score 0.19. One banner, and you're already in "needs improvement".

Bursts, not totals

Shifts that happen close together are grouped into a session window (gaps under 1 second, the window capped at 5 seconds). Your page's CLS is the score of its worst window, so one bad moment decides the number, no matter how long the user stays.

The usual culprits and their fixes

1. Images and videos without dimensions. The browser doesn't know how tall they'll be until they load.

<!-- The browser computes the aspect ratio from these and reserves the box -->
<img src="hero.jpg" width="1200" height="675" alt="…">

img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }   /* stays responsive, keeps the ratio */
.video-embed { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; width: 100%; }

2. Ads, embeds and iframes. Reserve the slot's most likely size:

.ad-slot { min-height: 250px; }   /* don't collapse it to 0 when there's no ad */

3. Content injected above what the user is reading (cookie banners, "download our app" bars, late-loading announcements). Put them in reserved space, overlay them (position: fixed), or insert them below the fold.

4. Web fonts swapping in. A fallback font with different letter widths reflows the text when the real font arrives. Preload the key font and match the fallback's size:

<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>

@font-face {
  font-family: 'Inter Fallback';
  src: local('Arial');
  size-adjust: 107%;   /* tune so Arial takes the same space as Inter */
}
body { font-family: 'Inter', 'Inter Fallback', sans-serif; }

5. Animating layout properties. Animating top, height or margin moves other elements. Animate transform instead: it moves pixels without changing layout, so it never counts as a shift.

Measure it in code

let cls = 0;
new PerformanceObserver(list => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    if (!entry.hadRecentInput) {   // shifts right after a tap/keypress don't count
      cls += entry.value;
      console.log('shift', entry.value.toFixed(3), entry.sources?.map(s => s.node));
    }
  }
}).observe({ type: 'layout-shift', buffered: true });

(This simple sum ignores session windows; for the real number use Google's web-vitals library: onCLS(console.log).)

See it yourself

  • DevTools → ⋮ → More tools → Rendering → tick Layout Shift Regions. Every shift flashes blue.
  • DevTools → Performance → record a page load → the Layout shifts track shows each one and which element moved.
  • Lighthouse / PageSpeed Insights → "Avoid large layout shifts" lists the guilty elements.

Real-world story

Yahoo! JAPAN News (over 22 billion page views a month) fixed late-loading images that shoved text down by reserving their space. Its layout-shift score dropped from about 0.2 to almost zero, and readers viewed about 15% more pages per session with 13% longer sessions. (Reel: The page that jumps under your thumb.)

Common mistakes

  • Testing only on a fast laptop. Shifts happen when things load late: test with Network throttling on "Slow 4G".
  • Setting height in CSS but width: 100%. The image stretches. Use width/height attributes plus height: auto, or aspect-ratio.
  • Collapsing empty ad slots. If no ad fills, keep the reserved space (or a placeholder), or the content jumps up.

Interview questions

What is CLS and what counts as a good score?

The largest burst of unexpected layout shifts during the page's life. Each shift = impact fraction × distance fraction. Good ≤ 0.1, needs improvement up to 0.25, poor above 0.25.

Does every movement count as a layout shift?

No. Shifts within 500 ms of a user input (tap, click, keypress) are expected and excluded. Movement done with CSS transform doesn't change layout, so it never counts. Content appearing at the end of the page without moving anything doesn't count either.

How do you prevent layout shift from images?

Always give width and height attributes (or CSS aspect-ratio) so the browser reserves the box before the image downloads; keep it responsive with max-width: 100%; height: auto.

A cookie banner is causing CLS. What are your options?

Make it an overlay (position: fixed), reserve its space from the first paint (render it server-side), or place it at the bottom where it doesn't push content.

title: INP
text: Input → next paint. Parts: input delay (main thread busy) + processing (handlers) + presentation delay (style/layout/paint). Roughly your worst interaction of the visit, not an average. Fix: feedback first, await scheduler.yield() , heavy work after; break long tasks. See it: Performance panel live metrics → interactions list. Trap: scroll and hover are not counted — only click, tap, key press.

TBT = sum over long tasks of (duration − 50 ms) between FCP and interactive. Lab stand-in for INP; Lighthouse weight 30% (largest). Puzzle: tasks 70, 140, 40 ms → TBT = 20 + 90 + 0 = 110 ms .

title: Critical rendering path
text: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM → render tree → first pixels. CSS is render-blocking ; plain <script> is parser-blocking . Shrink it: inline critical CSS, load the rest non-blocking, media="print" for non-critical sheets, defer scripts. See it: Lighthouse "Render blocking requests"; Performance panel request details "Render blocking". Trap: a script after a stylesheet waits for that CSS → CSS can block parsing too.

  • See it: Lighthouse "Render blocking requests"; Performance panel request details "Render blocking". Trap: a script after a stylesheet waits for that CSS → CSS can block parsing too.

title: async vs defer
text: plain: stop parsing, fetch, run. async : fetch in parallel, run on arrival, no order. defer : fetch in parallel, run after parsing, in document order, before DOMContentLoaded. defer → app code; async → independent scripts (analytics). type="module" is deferred by default. Trap: async scripts that depend on each other break randomly; defer does nothing on inline scripts.

title: What is state
text: State = data your UI remembers right now that can change while the page is open. Rule: if it changes and the screen must show it, it's state. React's idea: UI = f(state) . Trap: don't store what you can compute. const total = items.reduce(...) , not useState(total) → two sources of truth drift. title: React Query

Too little = screens lie; too much = refetch the world. Other tabs: refetch on window focus; BroadcastChannel ; server push (S6).

In the wild: GitHub (REST + GraphQL), Shopify Storefront (GraphQL), T3-stack apps (tRPC). Trap: GraphQL is not "faster" — fewer round trips, but careless queries are slow and you lose easy caching. Trap: no business rules (pricing etc.) in the BFF — they get copied per BFF and drift. BFF = shaping only.

Trap: offset is fine for rarely-changing data and jump-to-page UIs (admin tables, search results). It breaks on fast-changing feeds.

Trap: ties on the sort key skip rows → sort by (created_at, id) and put both in the cursor. Cost: no jump to page 50.

title: Waterfalls
text: Request 2 waits for request 1 → staircase in the Network waterfall; each step costs a round trip (~100–300 ms on mobile). Trap: true dependency (needs user id) → move the join to the server (one endpoint / BFF) so it happens next to the DB.

title: Parallel requests
text: Independent requests: start all, then await Promise.all([...]) → total ≈ slowest, not the sum. HTTP/2 multiplexes; HTTP/1.1 ≈ 6 connections per host. Promise.all rejects on the first failure (good results lost). Promise.allSettled → {status, value | reason} for each. Trap: await a(); await b(); await c(); is sequential. Create the promises first, then await them together.

title: Race conditions
text: Responses arrive in network order , not request order → an old, slow response can overwrite a newer one. React fix: let ignore = false; … if (!ignore) setX(d); return () => { ignore = true; } . Trap: debounce doesn't fix races (S3E23) — ignore or cancel stale requests; React Query keys data by query.

title: AbortController
text: const c = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: c.signal }); c.abort(); → really stops the request. In effects: abort in the cleanup; ignore AbortError (a cancel isn't a failure). title: Retries + backoff
text: Exponential backoff: 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s… capped. Add jitter (random delay) to avoid the thundering herd. Retry network errors, timeouts/408, 429 (after Retry-After), 5xx like 503. Don't retry 400/401/404. React Query: queries retry 3× with min(1000·2^n, 30000) by default; mutations retry 0×. Trap: retry a POST only with an idempotency key.

See it: api.github.com headers x-ratelimit-limit: 60 , x-ratelimit-remaining , x-ratelimit-reset (unauthenticated). On 429: read Retry-After and wait. Be a good client: debounce, dedupe, cache. Trap: boundaries don't catch event-handler or async errors → put the error in state and throw during render, or throwOnError in your data library.

title: Suspense boundaries

One boundary = waits for the slowest; one per component = popcorn + jumps. Group: critical first, own boundary for heavy parts, below-the-fold together. Pair each Suspense boundary with an ErrorBoundary. Trap: useEffect fetching never suspends → use use(promise) , a framework loader, or useSuspenseQuery .

title: How did it arrive?
text: HTTP is request → response: the server can't speak first. "Real-time" = the server can push the moment something happens. See it: WhatsApp Web → DevTools → Network → filter WS → click the connection → Messages . ↓ red = received, ↑ green = sent. Five transports: short polling · long polling · Server-Sent Events · WebSockets · WebRTC. Trap: "real-time means WebSockets" → no. Pick by who talks and how often (a badge can poll; AI answers stream over SSE).

title: Short polling
text: Ask on a fixed timer ("anything new?"). Cost = latency (up to one interval) + load (10,000 tabs ÷ 5 s = 2,000 req/s, mostly empty). Fine for rare updates where seconds of delay are OK: dashboards, build status, unread badges. Works through every proxy. Trap: setInterval(fetch) overlaps when the server slows → schedule the next poll with setTimeout after the response; skip work when document.hidden .

title: Long polling
text: Server holds the request open until there's news (or ~30 s timeout → empty response), client immediately asks again. Near-instant, plain HTTP. Costs: full request + headers per message, one open request per user. Trap: messages in the gap between polls → send a cursor ( ?since=<last id> ) so the server returns everything after it.

title: Server-Sent Events
text: One HTTP response that never ends: Content-Type: text/event-stream . Format: id: , event: , data: lines, blank line ends an event. new EventSource('/stream') → onmessage . Auto-reconnects and sends Last-Event-ID so the server can resume. Limits: one-way (send with normal fetch POST), text only. Trap: HTTP/1.1 ≈ 6 connections per origin; each open stream holds one → 7th tab hangs. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on one connection.

title: WebSockets
text: Starts as HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket → 101 Switching Protocols → same TCP connection carries frames both ways. Frame header 2–14 bytes vs hundreds of bytes of HTTP headers. wss:// = over TLS. API: onopen , send , onmessage , onclose . Each message is a task (S1E15) → batch bursts, render once per frame ( requestAnimationFrame ). Trap: WebSockets do not reconnect by themselves. Reconnect, catch up and resend are your job (E10).

title: WebRTC
text: Browser ↔ browser audio, video, data. See it: on a Meet call open chrome://webrtc-internals . Signaling (your choice, usually a WebSocket) swaps offer/answer (SDP) + ICE candidates . STUN = "what's my public address", TURN = relay when direct fails. Code: new RTCPeerConnection({ iceServers }) → createDataChannel / addTrack → createOffer → setLocalDescription → send via signaling. Trap: 100-person mesh = 99 uploads each. Big calls use an SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit): upload once, server forwards.

title: The showdown
text: Audio/video/peer data → WebRTC . 2. Client sends often, low latency (chat, games, cursors) → WebSockets . Server pushes, client listens (scores, notifications, AI answers) → SSE . 4. Rare updates / delay OK → polling (long polling if faster). SSE: one-way, built-in reconnect, text, plain HTTP. WS: two-way, binary, DIY reconnect, leaves HTTP after upgrade. Polling: most compatible, most wasteful. Trap: "chat needs WebSockets" → not necessarily: SSE down + POST up is valid and stays plain HTTP (caching, auth, load balancing).

  3. SSE: one-way, built-in reconnect, text, plain HTTP. WS: two-way, binary, DIY reconnect, leaves HTTP after upgrade. Polling: most compatible, most wasteful.
  4. Trap: "chat needs WebSockets" → not necessarily: SSE down + POST up is valid and stays plain HTTP (caching, auth, load balancing).

title: Heartbeats
text: A dead TCP connection doesn't announce itself (sleep, Wi-Fi drop) → half-open connection; app shows "online" forever. Proxies also kill idle connections. App-level ping/pong: every message resets a timer; silence > interval + margin (e.g. 35 s for 30 s pings) → ws.close() → reconnect. Browsers answer protocol ping frames silently, and JS can't send them → apps send their own {type:'ping'} . Trap: interval must be under the shortest idle timeout on the path (often 20–30 s), but not so fast it drains batteries.

Retry network errors (1006).

title: Acks & dedup
text: WhatsApp ticks: 1 grey = server got it, 2 grey = delivered to the device, 2 blue = read. Clock = pending (optimistic UI, S4E15). Lost ack → retry → duplicate. Trap: generate the id on the client : a server id doesn't exist until the first attempt succeeds.

title: Scaling WebSockets
text: Sockets are stateful: Alice on server A, Bob on server B. Fix: pub/sub (Redis, Kafka, NATS): A publishes to user:bob , B is subscribed and pushes down Bob's socket. Trap: sticky sessions only route reconnects to the same server; they don't deliver cross-server messages.
